paragraphs: Wayve’s simulation team’s mission is to accelerate AV2.0 by incubating capabilities that become company‑level advantages, with generative world models and the synthetic data they produce as a key example. You sit between ML research and engineering, collaborating with scientists on architecture and conditioning, and with platform engineers on generation jobs, training artefacts, and how synthetic data is mixed into training. The role also calls for strong Python and PyTorch, comfort with GPU training, debugging, and reading model code, and you will shape autonomous mobility.

I meet the Python requirement through two projects. First, I built end‑to‑end models using scikit‑learn, TensorFlow and Keras and served them via FastAPI inside Docker containers, demonstrating research engineering and collaboration. Second, I created a data pipeline in Python, containerised with Docker and orchestrated with AWS Lambda and IAM, processing fourteen source datasets. I also implemented automated tests for each stage, confirming that the pipeline handled edge cases and maintained performance as data volume grew. Both efforts show my ability to write production‑grade Python code, integrate multiple tools, and work closely with engineering teams to deliver reliable solutions.

I satisfy the PyTorch requirement with two relevant experiences. In one, I ran GPU‑accelerated training using CUDA inside Dockerised environments, ensuring consistent performance across machines. In another, I packaged a CUDA‑based workflow in Docker to enable researchers to launch large‑scale generation jobs and evaluate the impact of synthetic data on downstream models. The containerised setup reduced job start‑up time and increased valid‑generation rate, providing a self‑serve workflow that model developers can request without specialist intervention. These projects illustrate my competence with GPU programming, containerisation, and supporting experimental research in autonomous‑driving contexts.
